correctness.rationale: For a set with occupancies \(d_i\) and size \(s\), an outside vertex in part \(i\) has exactly \(s-d_i\) selected neighbors. This yields a necessary-and-sufficient occupancy criterion. Choosing an exact-three witness part leaves exactly three selected vertices outside it and reduces every existence instance to size at most \(6\). The four possible minimum sizes \(3,4,5,6\) are then exhausted by the distribution of those three outside vertices, giving the stated branches. Exhaustive occupancy enumeration through total order \(20\) and direct labeled-graph subset enumeration through order \(9\) match the formula exactly. Finite checks are corroborative, not the proof.

originality.rationale: The initiating 2025 source was inspected at the definition, complete-bipartite theorem, and conclusion. It gives \(\gamma_{\overline{3}}(K_{3,n})=3\) and \(\gamma_{\overline{3}}(K_{m,n})=6\) for \(m,n\ge4\), but no complete-multipartite theorem. Database searches using the exact defining phrase, proper-\(p\) aliases, secondary-domination terminology, and the complete-multipartite specialization returned no statement implying the displayed classification. The closest complete-multipartite records concern different domination invariants, whose hypotheses do not encode the required exact-three witness.
residual_risks: An older equivalent statement may exist under terminology not captured by the searched proper-domination, secondary-domination, or exact-neighbor aliases.

value.rationale: The initiating article introduces the invariant, gives exact biclique values only in selected regimes, and explicitly presents calculation of proper \(3\)-domination numbers on further graph classes as meaningful. The theorem gives a natural complete classification on the canonical complete-multipartite family, resolves all small-shore biclique boundary cases, identifies exactly when the parameter does not exist, and supplies the structural occupancy lemma that explains why no finite value above \(6\) can occur in this class.
